newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S., Britain signal readiness for Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain signal readiness for Zaire mission.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has tentatively agreed to U.S. participation in a multinational force to help some one million starving refugees in eastern Zaire and the Pentagon said the troops could go next week.

Momentum built up on Wednesday for the dispatch of the proposed force to the war-ravaged region as Britain also signalled readiness to send troops, but the mission faces potential perils in dealing with armed Hutu hardliners.

A United Nations envoy negotiating a mandate for the force with Rwanda and Zaire, whose army is battling Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels, said it was unclear how the Canadian-led troops could handle armed Hutus using refugees as a screen.
Most are former soldiers of the Rwanda Armed Forces (FAR) who fled with Hutu civilians after losing a civil war following the 1994 massacre of Tutsis in Rwanda.
The world community is eager to avoid a re-run of 1994 when it effectively fed and gave sanctuary to many of those responsible for the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 people, mainly Tutsis.
The Hutus fear revenge for the genocide and are apparently putting up a last stand at the teeming Mugunga refugee camp near Goma.
"We don't know what is the strength of the ex-FAR and the Interahamwe (Hutu miltia)," said U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien after talks in the Zairean capital Kinshasa on Wednesday.
"We don't know whether they will accept to be separated from their human shield," he told reporters.
Chretien said, however, that both Zaire and Rwanda were now agreed on the main objectives of the proposed international humanitarian intervention in the region.

"They are agreed...to help the Rwandan, Burundian or Zairean refugees on the ground on Zairean territory. They are agreed that this force should create the conditions for an eventual voluntary repatriation of the refugees to their countries of origin," he said.
"They are both agreed that if this force does not achieve the return of the refugees then it will have failed."
Until Wednesday Zaire had insisted that any aid for Rwandan refugees should be distributed only in Rwanda as a way of encouraging the refugees to return home.
It also opposed any dealings between aid agencies and Tutsi rebels who seized Zaire's two eastern provinces bordering Rwanda since fighting erupted on October 18.
A government spokesman denounced a deal between aid agencies and rebels which allowed a first consignment of aid to enter the city of Goma on Monday as a violation of Zaire's sovereignty.
Chretien was unable to specify whether the proposed multinational force would operate out of both Rwanda and Zaire.
But he said troops could be ready to act within a matter of days. Only a mandate from the U.N. Security Council was now needed.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment, expected to last about four months, involved sending 1,000 ground troops to Zaire. An additional 2,000 to 3,000 American troops would go to nearby countries to help with support activities, the Pentagon said.

"The president has decided that the United States is willing, in principle, to participate in a limited fashion in this mission as long as certain conditions are stipulated to," McCurry said at a White House briefing.
Among the conditions he listed were that the mission would be of limited duration and made up of a multinational force.
McCurry also said the mission would have to be "very clearly defined" and that it would not try to disarm militants or conduct any kind of "forced entry."
Canadian Army Lieutenant General Maurice Baril is due to lead the force.

"(U.S.) troops could be flowing into place sometime next week," said a senior Pentagon official, adding that the 1,000 troops in Zaire would include about 600 elite paratroopers from the U.S. 508th Airborne Infantry Regiment based at Vicenza, Italy.
The White House announcement cleared the way for the U.N. Security Council to work on a resolution, already drafted by Canada, in the hope that it can be adopted by the end of the week.
In London, Britain said it was ready to contribute troops but Prime Minister John Major said vital details about the international mission still needed to be worked out.

"Ministers agreed the UK should be ready to contribute constructively to the international response, including to a multinational force, providing a satisfactory plan can be worked out," said a statement from Major's office.
France, which led the intervention lobby but seen by Rwanda as partisan in the Hutu-Tutsi conflict, welcomed the new commitments.
